articles.title: Panama: Latin America & The Caribbean Weekly Situation Update as of 16 October 2026
articles.description: Please refer to the attached Infographic. KEY FIGURES 36K people left without power after severe weather in Chile 3.6K people remain in shelters after a 7.5 earthquake in Panama 4K homes damaged following 7.5 earthquake in Panama MEXICO: HURRICANES A new storm, Trudy, is forecast to strengthen into a Category 4 hurricane before passing off the coasts of Michoacán and Colima this weekend. Like Hurricanes Polo, Rachel and Simon before it, Trudy is tracking north-west along the coast. It would be the eighth major hurricane of a record eastern Pacific season, double the usual number, as record-warm waters linked to El Niño fuel storm activity. Hurricane Simon, which lingered off Jalisco, never made landfall, but its rain and storm surge damaged 71 homes and 35 businesses in Colima. It weakened to a tropical storm on 15 October and is forecast to drift towards Baja California Sur. Further north, the remnants of Rachel triggered floods that killed at least five people in Ensenada, Baja California, raising the death toll from the recent storms to six. As of 13 October, five more people remained missing in Baja California. CHILE: FLOODING A new frontal system swept across central Chile from 11 October, the 15th weather event linked to El Niño this year, according to the Government. The Mapocho River, which flows through the capital, Santiago, overflowed again, forcing a preventive evacuation of the Ribera del Río informal settlement in Talagante, south-west of the city. A weak tornado also damaged Santiago’s Alameda bus terminal in Estación Central. On 13 October, the storm left about 36,000 customers without power, 23,000 of them in the Santiago Metropolitan Region. As of 14 October, the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service reported 26 damaged homes between the Coquimbo and Maule regions, with 60 more in Rancagua awaiting assessment after flooding. The storm also forced 116 schools to suspend classes and put four health facilities in the capital region out of service. PANAMA: EARTHQUAKE Authorities have reported the first death following the 7.5 magnitude earthquake that struck Panama on 9 October, a person who was hospitalised with injuries. According to the National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC), the quake affected 13,623 people. A week later, at least 3,696 people remain in shelters, primarily in Veraguas, where 2,569 people are in shelters in Mariato, and Los Santos, with 644 people in 13 shelters. Many others remain with relatives or are sleeping outdoors for fear of aftershocks. Authorities report damage to more than 4,000 homes, 879 completely destroyed, 619 educational centres and 67 health centres. Rain, swollen rivers and landslides are hampering access to cut-off communities, where gaps in water and sanitation raise the risk of diarrhoeal disease. UNICEF estimates that nearly 38,000 people may need assistance, including about 8,300 children. HAITI: DROUGHT & FOOD INSECURITY Below-average rainfall over the past 45 days has degraded vegetation across southern Haiti, as an El Niño-related dry spell threatens the coming harvest. The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) reports the worst deterioration around Jacmel and Les Cayes and in parts of Ouest and Grand’Anse, where high temperatures are drying out soils and reducing water for irrigation. While northern Haiti received 25 to 50 per cent more rain than average from late August to early October, the south, especially Sud-Est, stayed dry, and forecasters expect below-average rainfall there to continue. FEWS NET warns that the dry conditions will likely reduce end-of-season yields, adding to the strain in a country where an estimated 3 - 3.5 million people already require food assistance.

articles.title: Sod’s law: what can two turf swaps 40 years apart tell us about Britain’s biodiversity crisis?
articles.description: In 1983, David Nash dug up a section of Kensington Gardens and swapped it with Welsh grassland. Four decades later, Mike Perry’s reverse swap revealed a striking reversal in the fortunes of urban and rural nature In 1983, an open-topped truck unloaded an unusual cargo in Kensington Gardens: 83 hunks of turf cut from Cae’n y Coed, a wooded hillside in the Ffestiniog valley. The ring of turf measuring eight metres in diameter that was removed from the park beside the Serpentine Gallery in west London to make space for the Welsh sods was then trucked from London to north Wales. So began Sod Swap, a piece of sculptural defiance by David Nash, which has had an unexpected and epic afterlife. More than 40 years later, photographic artist Mike Perry restaged the work as Reverse Sod Swap, exchanging exactly the same amount of turf between Springfield Park in Hackney, east London, and pastureland in Pembrokeshire, with strikingly different results. With twin works acquiring new relevance in a time of extinction and climate crises, the sod swapping is now the subject of a new book. Continue reading...

articles.title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
articles.description: Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction. Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range. Continue reading...

articles.title: What exactly is a Hi-Fi listening bar?
articles.description: Forget shouting over the music. At a Hi-Fi listening bar, you’re actually there to listen. Born in Japan and now popping up around the world, the concept puts vinyl, carefully tuned sound systems and intimate, low-lit spaces at the heart of a night out. At Saikindō in Abu Dhabi, the experience doesn’t stop at what comes through the speakers. Its cocktail menu takes songs apart and translates them into flavors you can drink. We spend a day there with Beverage Director and DJ Marco Corallo to find out why the world is tuning into listening bars, and what a favorite song might taste like in a glass.
